units.explanation: The PR removes the thread-ownership check from create_run, create_and_stream_run, and wait_for_run. The removed code verified `existing_thread.user_id != user.identity` and returned 404 for threads owned by another user. The downstream `_prepare_run` (run_preparation.py) never re-checks ownership: `_validate_resume_command` (lines 31-40) only checks thread existence/status, and `update_thread_metadata` (lines 103-157) only auto-creates a thread when it does not exist — when the thread already exists it updates metadata without verifying `thread.user_id == user.identity`. As a result, any authenticated user can now create a run on, and mutate the metadata of, a thread belonging to another user by supplying that user's thread_id. This is a newly introduced IDOR because the ownership guard that previously prevented it was deleted.

The DELETE /api_key/{api_key_id} route now authenticates the caller (get_current_active_user returns any active user) but no longer verifies that the caller owns the API key being deleted. The PR removed the ownership check `if api_key.user_id != user_id` from delete_api_key (crud.py) and removed the `current_user` parameter from the route, so any authenticated user can delete any other user's API key by supplying its UUID. This is an IDOR: the object is fetched by a user-controlled identifier (api_key_id) without verifying the requester owns it.

The PR removes the proxy-admin-only guard that prevented non-admins from modifying user roles in the single-user update path. The removed block (base lines 1134-1143) raised 403 'Only proxy admins can modify user roles' when user_request.user_role was set by a non-PROXY_ADMIN. After removal, _update_single_user_helper only enforces can_user_call_user_update (lines 1163-1172), which restricts updating OTHER users but does not restrict a user from changing their OWN role. Per policy, only proxy_admin can 'Manage team members and assign roles' and 'Create and manage all users'; internal_user 'Cannot add new users' and has no role-assignment rights. A non-admin can therefore self-escalate to proxy_admin via /user/update.
The PR removes the proxy-admin-only guard on the bulk_update 'all_users' path. The removed block (base lines 1521-1526) raised 403 'Only proxy admins can update all users at once' before the all-users branch. After removal, the branch at line 1516 executes prisma_client.db.litellm_usertable.update_many(where={}, data=non_default_values) (line 1554-1556) with no role check, so any authenticated user can update every user in the database, including setting user_role to proxy_admin. Policy reserves 'Create and manage all users' and role assignment to proxy_admin only.
The PR removes the proxy-admin-only guard that blocked non-admins from modifying user_role in bulk updates. The removed block (base lines 1508-1520) computed _bulk_role from data.user_updates or data.users and raised 403 'Only proxy admins can modify user roles' for non-PROXY_ADMIN. After removal, the per-user bulk path (data.users) flows into _update_single_user_helper, which no longer restricts role changes, so a non-admin can set user_role=proxy_admin on themselves or others. Policy limits role assignment to proxy_admin.
The PR narrows the admin-only guard on /key/update so that it only triggers when max_budget changes, removing the spend-change condition. The base code (lines 1964-1974) required _check_key_admin_access when either max_budget or spend was being modified. After the change (line 1965), a non-admin who passes the earlier common_key_access_checks and team-member permission checks can modify the key's spend field without any admin check, since the spend branch was deleted. Policy states only proxy_admin/team_admin/org_admin may modify budgets and spend; internal_user 'Cannot ... Modify budgets, rate limits, or settings'.

The newly added ajax_lookup endpoint (sqladmin/application.py:519-537) returns model data via loader.get_list(term) without any authentication or authorization check. Every other protected endpoint in the same class (list, create, details, delete, edit, export) is decorated with @login_required and calls a _<action> helper that enforces model_view.is_accessible(request) (e.g. _export at lines 225-230, _edit at 220-223). ajax_lookup has neither the @login_required decorator nor an is_accessible check, so it is reachable unauthenticated and bypasses the per-view access control. This violates the documented policy that is_accessible 'controls if this Model/View should be accessed' and that authenticate is 'called for validating each incoming request'.

The new MemoryViewSet.get_queryset() gates the entire memory listing on `self.request.user.is_superuser` (line 994), but the project's documented permission model defines a dedicated `memory.delete` permission (weblate/auth/data.py line 61, 'Delete translation memory') and the web views (weblate/memory/views.py lines 78, 94) authorize memory deletion via `check_perm(user, 'memory.delete', ...)`, not via superuser status. The API therefore uses an incorrect authorization check: a non-superuser who legitimately holds the `memory.delete` permission (per the documented fine-grained privilege system) is denied access to the memory API, while the check is inconsistent with the rest of the app. This is an incorrect authorization condition (CWE-863) in the newly added code.

The new `download` action fetches a CachedFile solely by a user-controlled UUID (`kwargs['cfid']`) via `get_object_or_404(CachedFile, id=kwargs['cfid'])` and returns its file contents. The CachedFile model (src/pretix/base/models/base.py:21-30) has no event/organizer/user scoping field, and the view performs no ownership or permission check tying the file to the requester's event/organizer. The `permission = 'can_view_orders'` attribute on the viewset only authorizes access to the exporter endpoint, not to an arbitrary CachedFile. Since the cfid is a random UUID returned to the user who initiated the export, any authenticated user with can_view_orders on any event can enumerate/guess other users' export file IDs and download their exported order data. This is a newly introduced endpoint (the whole file is added in this PR), so the flaw is newly exposed by this change.

The PR changes delete_realm_export to fetch the export by a user-controlled id without scoping to the requester's realm: `export_row = RealmExport.objects.get(id=export_id)` (line 99). The RealmExport model has a `realm` field (used in export_realm at line 68-74 and in do_delete_realm_export via `export_row.realm`), and the base version correctly scoped the lookup to the caller's realm (`realm=user.realm`). The new code only checks the export's status, so a realm admin in one organization can pass an export_id belonging to another organization and delete that other realm's export tarball (do_delete_realm_export calls delete_export_tarball on export_row.export_path). This is an IDOR: the object is fetched by a user-controlled identifier without verifying the requester's realm owns it.

The new ShareLinkViewSet exposes ShareLink objects via a ModelViewSet (retrieve/update/destroy by id) using PaperlessObjectPermissions. That permission backend (src/documents/permissions.py:31-38) returns True for ANY object that lacks an owner: `if hasattr(obj, 'owner') and obj.owner is not None: ... else: return True  # no owner`. The ShareLink model (src/documents/models.py:680) is a plain models.Model with no `owner` field, so every ShareLink is treated as 'unowned' and accessible to any authenticated user. Combined with the list filter ObjectOwnedOrGrantedPermissionsFilter (src/documents/filters.py:169-173), which unions in `queryset.filter(owner__isnull=True)`, the list endpoint returns ALL share links to any authenticated user. A user can therefore enumerate and read other users' share links (including their `slug`, which is the secret token used to access the shared document) — an IDOR / broken object-level authorization. The serializer also exposes the `slug` field, making the secret token directly readable.

RepsConfigViewSet.get_queryset returns RepsConfig.objects.all() with no ownership filter, unlike every sibling config viewset which filters by slot_config__slot__day__routine__user=self.request.user. RepsConfig extends AbstractChangeConfig, which has a slot_config FK (abstract_config.py:41-44) and therefore a get_owner_object() chain (SlotConfig.get_owner_object returns self.slot.day.routine, slot_config.py:141-145). WgerPermission.has_object_permission (permissions.py:43-58) only allows non-safe methods when owner_object.user == request.user, so a user can read (GET) any other user's RepsConfig objects via the list endpoint, and the queryset is not scoped to the requester. This is a newly introduced endpoint in the PR, exposing other users' private workout configuration data.
MaxRepsConfigViewSet.get_queryset returns MaxRepsConfig.objects.all() with no ownership filter. MaxRepsConfig extends AbstractChangeConfig (reps_config.py:29-33), which has a slot_config FK and a get_owner_object() chain, so WgerPermission.has_object_permission only permits non-safe methods for the owner. As a result, any authenticated user can read (GET) all other users' MaxRepsConfig objects through this newly added list endpoint, leaking private workout configuration data.
